I have worked in compliance for two years.
I drafted my first contract in English last year.
Have you been to London before?
We have just opened an office in the United States.
You have come a long way for a two-day conference. What brought you over?
My company is opening an office in the United States, so I have spent six months drafting contracts in English. I wanted to hear people who do it for a living.
You are in-house, then. So am I — I have been in-house counsel at an energy group for four years, and I still miss the firm on the quiet days.
There are not many quiet days on my side. Compliance, contracts, and whatever the board decides is urgent that week.
That sounds familiar. So — what has struck you most so far?
Honestly, the keynote. She touched on cross-border compliance for about four minutes and I wanted the whole hour on that.
She always does that. If you want it unpacked, the panel after lunch is the one to go to — my counterpart in Chicago is on it.
Then I will be there. And I will find you afterwards, if that is all right — I would like to hear how you got from the firm to in-house.

Good morning, and welcome to the second day of the Cross-Border Counsel Forum. My name is Ruth and I chair the programme committee. Three things before we start. The keynote has moved to the main hall at half past nine, because the room we booked yesterday was far too small, and I am told it was standing room only. The afternoon runs in three parallel panels, and the one on compliance in Latin America has already filled up, so please register at the desk if you have not done that yet. Finally, the delegate list is now on the app, with everybody's employer and city. If you have come here to meet your counterpart in another country, this is the morning to do it. Coffee is outside, and we start in twenty minutes.

The hardest question at any conference is not a legal one. It is: so, what did you think? And I have watched very competent people go completely blank on it, in their own language. Here is what I tell junior lawyers. Do not try to summarise the whole day. Pick one thing. Say what it was, say why it stayed with you, and say what you would do differently on Monday because of it. Thirty seconds, three moves. If you genuinely have nothing, be honest and turn the question round: name the session you are still thinking about, and ask what struck them. Nobody has ever minded that. The people who sound impressive at these events are not the ones with the most to say. They are the ones who decided, before they walked in, that one clear point beats four vague ones.
